According to a report commissioned by Robert Fleming Securities and Mintel International, the estimated 35bn stg earned by beneficiaries of building society windfall payments should prove to be a benefit to imports rather than a further call for an inflation rise. The report concludes people will spend nearly 8.2bn stg of their windfalls, or 23.2 per cent of the total sum, 2.1bn stg of which will be spent on holidays, another 2.1bn stg of which will go to furniture, carpets and other household appliances, and an additional 800m stg to be spent on items such as vehicles and electrical goods.
-- EUROPEAN MARKETS TO COME UNDER PRESSURE

After enjoying the day off on Friday for Assumption Day, Europe's stock markets are expected to experience a significant drop on Monday, following Friday's 3.1 per cent fall in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The European markets which remained open on Friday - in Amsterdam and Frankfurt - fell four per cent and 2.8 per cent respectively, with Paris, Rome and Milan expected to open Monday with their own heavy losses. The FTSE is expected to open down between 50 and 100 points.
-- FRUIT PRICES SET TO RISE AFTER POOR CROP IN MEDITERRANEAN

Due to the Mediterranean's worst crop results in over a decade, European Union member states are expected to face substantial increases in the price of fresh and processed fruits. A late-April frost and heavy winds in June have left farmers to predict the number of peach, apple and pear crops will be 60 per cent below average this year. Though the strength of sterling has helped keep UK prices in check, analysts have not ruled out the possibility of an eventual sharp increase in the cost of fruit.
-- US SUPPLIER SUED OVER 'MILLENNIUM BOMB' TILL

Mark Yarsike, the owner of a small Detroit Supermarket, is suing Atlanta-based cash register supplier Tec-America, because he claims its machines cease to operate once a customer attempts to use a credit card which expires after 2000. Yarsike claims to have experienced 150 cash register failures over the last three years, causing chaos in his three stores and losing him hundreds of thousands of dollars in the process.

Fast-growing Mexican media group Television Azteca has overcome a dispute with US television network NBC to make it Mexico's most successful initial public offering since the peso was devalued in 1994. Azteca shares ended their first day of trading at $19 3/16, up 5.14 per cent, attracting a significant amount of interest from investors enthused with Mexico's economic fundamentals and the growth prospects of Azteca.

Shareholders in Albert Fisher are awaiting the confirmation of the group's plan to sell its seafood division for up to 100m stg, as it has been interpreted as the beginning of the group's break- up. Shares in Fisher have struggled in recent years, with the appointment of Stephen Walls to chairman in 1992 having had a significant impact on the business, but little on stock value. Merrill Lynch analyst Tim Potter concluded Fisher's management 'is under pressure to come up with innovative measures to resto re some value to shareholders'.
